cases.text: If the same request lands twice - say the app retried after a timeout even though the server had actually finished, or someone tapped Pay two times - the end result should be as if it only happened once.
credits: repeating an operation has the same intended effect
users double-click, and clients time out
cases.notes: Same-effect-as-once plus the real-world sources of duplicates (retry after timeout, double tap), in own words.

cases.text: Think of a lift call button: mash it five times and one lift still comes. An API call should work the same way, because in real life stuff gets sent twice all the time - flaky wifi resends, impatient people double-tap, a client gives up waiting after the server already did the job.
credits: repeating an operation has the same intended effect
users double-click, and clients time out
cases.notes: Lift-button analogy carries the same-effect idea and the learner names retries, double taps and timeouts as the reason.

cases.text: Idempotency is when the client automatically sends the request again if it fails, and keeps trying until the server finally answers.

misconceptions.claim: repeating an operation has the same intended effect

cases.notes: Describes the act of retrying instead of the property that a repeat has the same effect as one call - a confusion with Retry.

cases.text: It's like an elevator door: each time someone else steps in, the countdown restarts, and it only shuts once nobody has come in for a few seconds. Same with a search box - you fire the lookup after the person pauses typing, not on every letter, so the heavy work doesn't run constantly.
credits: until a burst of events has been quiet
avoids firing expensive work for every keystroke
cases.notes: Elevator analogy captures the reset-until-quiet delay, and the search-box part gives the purpose of not doing heavy work per keystroke.

cases.text: i think it's something about waiting a little before running a function? like so it doesn't do too much work maybe
cases.notes: Gestures at waiting and saving work but never says the wait is until events stop; too vague to trust.

cases.text: Authentication is where the app checks what you're allowed to do, like whether you can edit a post or only look at it.

misconceptions.claim: verifying who a user or service is

cases.notes: Describes deciding permissions, which is authorization, not verifying identity.

cases.text: Obviously authentication is the permissions layer: once the system has your role, it works out exactly which actions and resources you're allowed.

misconceptions.claim: verifying who a user or service is

cases.notes: Confidently equates authentication with the permission check (authorization).

cases.text: Think of a bouncer checking your ID at the door: it's only about proving you really are who you claim to be - password, face scan, a code texted to your phone. The app has to be sure of that before it lets you near anything.
credits: verifying who a user or service is
the system needs a trustworthy identity
cases.notes: Bouncer analogy gives identity verification and that a trustworthy identity must come before any access.

cases.text: Proving you are who you say you are, e.g. logging in with a password.
credits: verifying who a user or service is
cases.notes: Identity verification is right, but it does not say a trusted identity is needed before access is granted.

cases.text: CORS is a firewall on the server that blocks requests coming from other domains, and it stops everything - browsers, curl, Postman, mobile apps - from calling your API unless you whitelist them.

misconceptions.claim: A browser-enforced policy that controls whether
does not stop non-browser clients

cases.notes: Two wrong ideas: it is a server-side request blocker rather than browser-enforced read control, and it supposedly stops non-browser clients too.

cases.text: CORS is how the backend checks who is calling it - it verifies the user's identity before it agrees to send the data back.

misconceptions.claim: controls whether frontend JavaScript can read responses

cases.notes: Treats CORS as identity verification; the source says it is browser read control and explicitly not authentication.

cases.text: it's a login token that's encrypted, which keeps the info inside private from the browser and from anyone snooping on the traffic i believe

misconceptions.claim: claim containers, not automatically encrypted

cases.notes: Hedged, but still asserts the token's contents are encrypted and private.

cases.text: It's a small token in three dot-separated chunks - header, payload, signature. Because of the signature, whoever receives it can check the data really came from the issuer it trusts and wasn't changed, without hitting the database every time. Anyone can still decode and read the middle bit, though.
credits: compact signed token format containing claims
claims were issued by a trusted signer
cases.notes: Gives the signed three-part format and the verify-without-lookup purpose, and correctly notes it is readable (not encrypted).

cases.text: A JWT is a signed token carrying claims like the user id and expiry, and the API doesn't need a DB lookup to trust it - because it's encrypted, so the client can't read or fake anything inside.

misconceptions.claim: claim containers, not automatically encrypted

credits: compact signed token format containing claims
cases.notes: Conclusion (signed claims, trusted without a lookup) is right, but the reason offered is encryption, which contradicts the source; the signature is what makes it trustworthy.

cases.text: it's the thing where the password gets turned into a random-looking string so it isn't stored as is. i think you can't really get it back? not totally sure
cases.notes: Right direction (not stored as-is, maybe irreversible) but one-way is only guessed at and fixed-length output and slow salting are absent.

cases.text: You lock the data up with a key so it's gibberish to everyone else, and whoever holds the right key can unlock it back to exactly what it was - unlike a hash, which you can't undo.
credits: A reversible transformation that protects data
cases.notes: Keyed, reversible protection of data, contrasted correctly with one-way hashing.

cases.text: Indexes = quicker searches. How it works: the DB remembers the results of previous queries, so the second time you ask it just returns the saved result.
credits: make particular lookups or orderings faster
cases.notes: Same right conclusion with the same wrong caching mechanism.

cases.text: A closure is when you have a function inside another function. It has something to do with scope.
cases.notes: Names nesting and scope but not the key relationship: keeping access to the variables where the function was created.

cases.text: Any instance can answer the next request, and that's because stateless servers are lighter and faster since they basically don't use memory.
credits: Any replica can serve the next request
cases.notes: Any-instance conclusion is right, but the reason (lighter, faster, no memory use) is wrong; it works because request state lives outside the instance.

cases.text: Instead of making one server beefier, you just add more servers running the same app.
credits: capacity by adding more instances or machines
cases.notes: Adding machines is right, but nothing about higher throughput or redundancy beyond one box.

cases.text: You grow by adding more machines to the pool - so you might go from a handful of instances to dozens of them.
credits: capacity by adding more instances or machines
cases.notes: Adds machines to grow capacity; no mention of throughput or resilience beyond one box.

cases.text: Horizontal scaling means upgrading your server - more RAM, a faster CPU - so the same machine can handle more users.

misconceptions.claim: capacity by adding more instances or machines

cases.notes: Upgrading one machine's RAM/CPU is vertical scaling; horizontal adds more instances.

cases.text: Vertical scaling is just upgrading your server's hardware, and it's the best approach because there's no ceiling - you can keep adding RAM forever - and having one really powerful machine gets rid of the single point of failure.

misconceptions.claim: has hardware and availability limits
can preserve a single point of failure

credits: Increasing the CPU, RAM, or resources
cases.notes: Definition right, but claims no limits and that one big box removes the single point of failure - both contradict the source.

cases.text: An access token is the long-lasting one you keep for weeks and use to get new tokens without logging in again. Making it last longer is actually safer, since you're not sending your password around.

misconceptions.claim: usually with a relatively short lifetime
reduce damage if the token is stolen

cases.notes: Describes the refresh token (long-lived, used to get new tokens) and claims longer lifetimes are safer, the opposite of the source.

cases.text: A refresh token lets the app grab a fresh access token without making you log in again - it works because your password is saved inside it, so the server just logs you in again automatically.
credits: used to obtain new access tokens
cases.notes: Getting new access tokens without a new sign-in is right, but the mechanism (it contains your password) is invented.

cases.text: When the access token dies, the refresh token gets you a new one with no login screen. That's possible because the refresh token is basically your password in encrypted form, which the auth server re-checks each time.
credits: used to obtain new access tokens
cases.notes: Same right conclusion; same wrong reason (it is the user's stored password).

cases.text: It's what quietly gets you a new access token so you're not kicked back to sign-in; my understanding is it holds your username and password and just replays them.
credits: used to obtain new access tokens
cases.notes: Hedged version: right outcome, wrong credential-replay mechanism.

cases.text: each client only gets so many requests per time period; go over and you're blocked for a bit
credits: how frequently a client, identity, or key
cases.notes: Same definition in casual words, still no purpose.

cases.text: It stops calling a dependency that keeps failing and tries it again later. The point is that otherwise the failed responses would get cached and served to users.
credits: Stop calling a failing dependency temporarily
cases.notes: The behaviour is right, but the reason (avoiding cached error responses) is not the source's reason of protecting resources from repeated slow failures.

cases.text: You retry after the same fixed wait every time, like 2 seconds, 2 seconds, 2 seconds. And the jitter is what makes all the clients retry at exactly the same moment, so the server can deal with them in one go.

misconceptions.claim: where delays grow after consecutive failures,
prevents many clients from retrying in lockstep.

cases.notes: Two wrong ideas: delays stay fixed instead of growing, and jitter is said to synchronize clients, the reverse of what it does.

cases.text: Exponential growth is when something keeps doubling, like compound interest or bacteria splitting in a petri dish.
cases.notes: True statement about exponential growth in general; nothing about retries, delays or protecting a recovering service.

cases.text: useMemo is for performance, it memoizes things so the app is faster.
cases.notes: Knows it is a performance tool but not what is cached (a calculation result) or when it is recomputed (dependencies change).

cases.text: i think it's used to speed up components, like memoization? so things don't slow down
cases.notes: Hedged version of the same vague speed-up idea.

cases.text: Controlled components are considered better practice than class components and they make your code cleaner and easier to test.
cases.notes: Plausible-sounding opinion mixing in class components; nothing about state driving the element's value.

cases.text: The browser's own input holds whatever the user typed, and you only peek at it through a ref when you need it, like on submit. Less wiring for a quick little form, and handy when some non-React script is also poking at the field.
credits: keeps its current value primarily in the DOM,
reduce plumbing for simple forms
cases.notes: Value lives in the DOM and is read through a ref, plus both purposes: less plumbing for simple forms and non-React integration.

cases.text: One part of the system drops jobs into a line and some other worker picks them up and does them whenever it gets to them.
credits: producers enqueue messages/jobs and consumers process them later.
cases.notes: Producer/consumer buffering is right, but not why: decoupling request latency from background work and smoothing bursts.

cases.text: The API just drops the task onto the queue and a worker handles it later, so the user gets a quick response instead of waiting for the email to go out. The reason that's faster, as far as I know, is that queues talk over a special binary protocol that's way lighter than HTTP, so the work itself takes less time to do - which is why every big company uses them.
credits: producers enqueue messages/jobs and consumers process them later.
cases.notes: Enqueue-then-worker and the quick response are right, but the explanation (a lighter binary protocol makes the work faster) is a non-sequitur; the gain comes from decoupling.

cases.text: The page is about how a model is a simpler version of something, which I guess matters a lot in computer science generally.
cases.notes: Hedged restatement of the title; no rubric idea is expressed.

cases.text: React uses a virtual DOM and was made by Facebook; it's the most popular front-end library out there.
cases.notes: General React trivia; nothing about components, rendering or committing as this page teaches them.

cases.text: components and rendering stuff
cases.notes: Just names topics from the page; no understanding shown.

cases.text: A closure remembers its surrounding bindings.
credits: plus access to the lexical variables
cases.notes: States the core idea (a closure keeps access to the variables of the scope it was created in) in its own words, but says nothing about what closures are for, so mostlyUnderstood rather than understood.

cases.text: A refresh token is a longer-lasting credential that gets you new access tokens without logging in again.
credits: used to obtain new access tokens
cases.notes: Gives the whole definition (a longer-lived credential that obtains new access tokens without signing in again) but not why it exists, the balance with short-lived access credentials, so mostlyUnderstood.

cases.text: Idempotency makes retries dangerous.

misconceptions.claim: Idempotency makes retries safe

cases.notes: Swaps one word of the source's statement that idempotency makes retries safe, asserting the opposite.

cases.text: Nobody holding a JWT can read the claims in its payload.

misconceptions.claim: signed claim containers, not automatically encrypted

cases.notes: Claims the payload cannot be read, but the source says JWTs are signed and not automatically encrypted, so a holder can read the claims.

cases.text: Throttling waits until the events stop coming and only then runs the handler once.

misconceptions.claim: once per time window while events continue

cases.notes: Describes debouncing (wait until the events stop, then run once) instead of throttling, which runs at most once per window while events continue.

cases.text: Repeating an idempotent operation does not have the same effect as doing it once.

misconceptions.claim: repeating an operation has the same intended effect

cases.notes: The negation turns the definition into its opposite, since the source says repeating the operation has the same intended effect as doing it once.

cases.text: Retrying a failed call always makes it succeed eventually, whatever the error.

misconceptions.claim: Transient network/service errors often succeed later

cases.notes: Turns the source's qualified claim (transient errors often succeed later, retry when the failure may be temporary) into guaranteed success for any error.

cases.text: You try a failed call again when the failure might only be temporary.
credits: again when the failure may be temporary
cases.notes: Correctly qualified restatement of the definition (retry when the failure may be temporary), but the reason, that transient errors often succeed later, is missing, so mostlyUnderstood.

cases.text: Big tables are usually the slow ones, so a table's size is what an index shrinks to make lookups fast.

misconceptions.claim: trade additional storage and write cost

cases.notes: From the plausible observation that big tables are slow it concludes that an index shrinks the table, whereas the source says an index costs additional storage and write cost to make reads faster.

cases.text: Calls that fail at night tend to succeed in the morning, so the time of day is what makes a retry work.

misconceptions.claim: Transient network/service errors often succeed later

cases.notes: Treats a correlation (night failures, morning successes) as the cause, whereas the source says retries work because transient errors often succeed later, not because of the time of day.

cases.text: An access token is a longer-lived credential used to obtain new refresh tokens.

misconceptions.claim: longer-lived credential used to obtain new access tokens

cases.notes: Swaps the two tokens: in the source the refresh token is the longer-lived credential used to obtain new access tokens, not the other way round.

cases.text: Authorization is what an allowed identity uses to decide who it is.

misconceptions.claim: deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed

cases.notes: Reverses the definition (authorization decides what an authenticated identity may do) into an allowed identity deciding who it is, which is really authentication.

cases.text: An index speeds up lookups on a column, because the database keeps the results of earlier queries and hands them back.
credits: make particular lookups or orderings faster
cases.notes: Right that an index speeds up lookups, but the reason given (reusing cached results of earlier queries) is a cache, not the maintained data structure the source describes, though no source sentence is directly contradicted.

cases.text: A refresh token gets you a new access token without logging in again, because your password is stored inside it.
credits: used to obtain new access tokens
cases.notes: Right that a refresh token gets a new access token without signing in again, but the reason (the password is stored inside it) is wrong and not supported by the source, which calls it a separate longer-lived credential.

cases.text: Authentication checks who you are; authorization then decides what you may do.
credits: verifying who a user or service is
the system needs a trustworthy identity
cases.notes: Correctly says authentication verifies who you are and that authorization only comes afterwards to decide permissions, covering both the definition and the identity-before-access constraint.

cases.text: Debouncing waits for a pause in the events, while throttling runs at most once per window.
credits: until a burst of events has been quiet
cases.notes: Captures debouncing as waiting for a pause in the events and contrasts it correctly with throttling, but omits the purpose (not firing expensive work on every keystroke), so mostlyUnderstood.

cases.text: Idempotency is about retries.
cases.notes: Only links idempotency to retries without saying what the property is; torn between fragile and insufficient, I chose the less generous insufficient because a teacher cannot tell what is understood.

cases.text: JWTs are really popular and lots of web frameworks support them.
cases.notes: True-sounding remarks about popularity and framework support say nothing the source teaches about JWTs (signed claims verified without a database lookup).

cases.text: Marking a cookie HttpOnly makes XSS attacks harmless.

misconceptions.claim: it does not eliminate XSS impact

cases.notes: The source says HttpOnly reduces exposure of session secrets but does not eliminate XSS impact, so calling XSS harmless contradicts it.

cases.text: Pressing an elevator call button five times still brings just one elevator.
cases.notes: An apt everyday example of repeating an action with the same effect as doing it once, but the general property and why it matters for retries are never stated; torn with mostlyUnderstood, so the less generous fragile.

cases.text: It's fast.
cases.notes: Two words with no stated subject say nothing about what an index is or how it speeds up lookups.

cases.text: A JWT is a compact token with a header, a payload and a signature. The signature lets the API check who issued it without looking anything up in a database. Because it is encrypted, nobody can read the claims inside.

misconceptions.claim: signed claim containers, not automatically encrypted

credits: compact signed token format containing claims
without a database lookup for every verification
cases.notes: The structure and the lookup-free verification are right, but the confident last clause that the token is encrypted and unreadable contradicts the source's signed, not automatically encrypted.

cases.text: A stateless server handles each request without relying on anything kept in its own memory, so any replica can take the next request, which makes horizontal scaling easier; that is also why stateless servers never need a database.

misconceptions.claim: keep request state outside a specific instance

credits: can handle each request without relying on
Any replica can serve the next request
cases.notes: Definition and the replica/scaling mechanism are right, but the final clause wrongly concludes that stateless servers never need a database, whereas the source keeps request state outside the instance.

cases.text: It keeps it so that it doesn't have to make it again.
cases.notes: Every noun is a pronoun, so a teacher cannot tell whether the learner knows useCallback caches a function reference until its dependencies change; torn with fragile, so the less generous insufficient.

cases.text: It keeps them around after it finishes so that it can use them.
cases.notes: Gestures at variables surviving after a function finishes, but the pronouns hide which function keeps them and which one finishes; torn with fragile, so the less generous insufficient.

cases.text: Authentication is when the system confirm who you are, a person or also a service that call the API. It must be sure your identity is real and can be trusted before to give you any access. Is like passport control in airport: before anything else, they check that you are really you.
credits: verifying who a user or service is
the system needs a trustworthy identity
cases.notes: Both rubric ideas, verifying who a user or service is and needing a trusted identity before any access, are stated correctly in non-native English with a passport-control analogy, and nothing is wrong.

cases.text: Authorization is the step after a successful login. Once the password and MFA check passes, the server knows exactly who the user is, and a verified identity can be trusted, so the user is cleared for any action. Later requests don't need re-checking either, since the login already settled permissions.

misconceptions.claim: Identity alone is not permission
authorization still happens per action/resource

cases.notes: From the true premise that login verifies identity it wrongly concludes the user may do any action and that later requests need no check, contradicting 'identity alone is not permission' and per-action authorization.

cases.text: Authentification is when the system decide what the user have the right to do. For exemple a normal user can read the reports but the admin can also delete acounts, so it depends of the role that you have.

misconceptions.claim: verifying who a user or service is

cases.notes: It gives authorization's meaning (deciding what a user may do by role, with the reports/admin example) as the definition of authentication and never mentions verifying identity, a confusion with Authorization.

cases.text: Hotel version: the front desk checking your ID is authentication. Authorization is what your key card then opens, your room but not the staff office. Knowing who you are doesn't get you in everywhere, and each door checks the card again. So: deciding what an identified person may do, door by door.
credits: deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed
Identity alone is not permission
authorization still happens per action/resource
cases.notes: Through a hotel key-card analogy it states that authorization decides what an identified person may do, that knowing who you are does not open every door, and that each door is checked, with nothing wrong.

cases.text: ok so authorization = deciding what you're allowed to do once the system already knows who you are. authentication has to go first, and I think that's for speed: checking a password is quick and cheap, permission checks are the heavy part, so you run the cheap filter first to save server load.
credits: deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed
cases.notes: The definition and the order (authentication first) are right, but the order is justified by server cost instead of authorization needing an authenticated identity, a reason the source does not support, so weak reasoning rather than understood.

cases.text: An error boundary catches errors from the components inside it and renders a fallback UI instead. So once your components are wrapped, nothing can crash the app anymore: even a failed fetch in a click handler or an error in a setTimeout just ends up in the fallback. Every error gets handled for you.

misconceptions.claim: catches certain render/ lifecycle errors in descendants

cases.notes: From the true premise that a boundary catches its children's errors it concludes that every error, even in click handlers and timers, is caught and nothing can crash the app, overgeneralizing 'certain render/lifecycle errors'.

cases.text: Error boundaries work like fuses in a house: one circuit shorts, that room goes dark, not the whole building. Wrap part of the React tree in one, and if something in there throws while rendering, only that part shows a fallback. They won't catch every error though, just certain render or lifecycle ones.
credits: catches certain render/ lifecycle errors in descendants
One broken widget should not necessarily
cases.notes: A fuse-box analogy plus a plain statement cover both rubric ideas, that only the failing subtree shows a fallback instead of the whole app and that only certain rendering/lifecycle errors are caught, with nothing wrong.

cases.text: Unit test is when you test one small function alone, so it never can touch a real dependancy: every thing it uses must be always mocked, the database, the clock, other classes, everything. If not, is not a unit test anymore.

misconceptions.claim: small behavior, usually with controlled dependencies

cases.notes: It reasons from 'one small function alone' to the rule that every dependency must always be mocked, turning the source's 'usually with controlled dependencies' into an absolute.

cases.text: Its a test for one small peice of behaviour, like checking calculateTotal([10,5]) gives 15. You usually swap the real dependencies (db, network) for fakes so you're only testing that bit of logic in isolation.
credits: A focused test of a small behavior
cases.notes: The focused test of one small behaviour with dependencies usually faked is right, but the purpose (fast feedback on logic and edge cases) is never given, so it stops at mostly understood.

cases.text: Open/closed means adding new behaviour by extending, like plugging in a new class, instead of editing the core switch again and again. People say it lowers regression risk, but I reckon that's just correlation: teams using it are more senior and would have fewer regressions anyway. The principle itself doesn't reduce anything.

misconceptions.claim: It can reduce regression risk

credits: new behavior through extension without repeatedly modifying
cases.notes: Extension instead of repeatedly editing central logic is right, but it recasts the source's causal claim that the principle can reduce regression risk as mere correlation with senior teams and denies any effect.

cases.text: Think of a vending machine: you get a coin slot and some buttons, but you can't reach in and rearrange the snacks. Encapsulation is that for code: the class keeps its guts private and only offers the few actions callers need, like cart.addItem() instead of pushing into cart.items directly.
credits: expose only the operations consumers need
cases.notes: Hiding internals and offering only the operations callers need is right (vending-machine analogy), but it never says why, i.e. keeping distant code from depending on fragile details, so the purpose is missing.

cases.text: Cohesion is how well the jobs inside one module fit together. When they fit, the module is easier to read and maintain. I know that from my old job: our cohesive modules were also the ones with the fewest bugs, so clearly the cohesion is what made them easy to work with.
credits: responsibilities inside one module belong together
High cohesion makes modules easier to understand
cases.notes: The definition and the maintainability conclusion are right, but the only support is that cohesive modules also had fewer bugs, a co-occurrence taken as proof of cause, so weak reasoning is the less generous and fitting label.

cases.text: The .d.ts is a file for TypeScript where are the types of one library. When you install a library of JavaScript you need also this file, and then it works better with the compiler.
cases.notes: It links the file to a JavaScript library's types and the compiler but never says it holds declarations without implementation or what it describes, and 'it works better' is vague, so the central idea is only gestured at.

cases.text: A .d.ts file just has type declerations, no real implementation inside. Thats because the bundler strips the function bodies out when minifying, to keep the bundle small, so only the types are left for the compiler.
credits: type declarations without runtime implementation
cases.notes: Right that a .d.ts holds only type declarations with no implementation, but the reason given, a bundler stripping function bodies when minifying, is invented and unsupported by the source.

cases.text: Open/closed is just the O in SOLID.
cases.notes: Placing the principle in SOLID is true but not what the source teaches here, so nothing shows whether the learner knows about extending instead of modifying central logic.
